segments.caption: z-test, t-test, chi-square, ANOVA. Which one should you use?
Pick the wrong test, and your answer is wrong. This one video tells you exactly which test to use. Save it!
Choosing a test comes down to two questions.
One: what kind of data? Numbers you can average, like weight or time? Or categories you count, like tea or coffee?
Two: how many groups are you comparing?
z-test.
Compare one average with a claim, when sigma, the population's spread, is known, or the sample is large.
Do these juice bottles really hold 200 ml? We checked 100 of them.
One-sample t-test.
Same question, but the sample is small and sigma is unknown. That's most of real life.
Do these 10 phones really last 20 hours, like the ad says?
Two-sample t-test.
Two separate groups. Are their averages different?
Battery life of brand A, versus brand B.
Paired t-test.
The same people, measured twice: before and after.
Typing speed before a course, and after it.
ANOVA.
Three or more groups. Is any of their averages different?
Waiting times at three coffee shops.
Chi-square test of independence.
Now the data are categories. Are two of them linked?
Does preferring tea or coffee depend on age?
Chi-square goodness of fit.
One category. Do the counts match what you expected?
Is this dice fair? Roll it 60 times, and count each face.
Bonus interview tip: t-tests and ANOVA assume the data are roughly normal.
Small sample, heavily skewed? Swap them: Mann-Whitney for the two-sample t-test, Wilcoxon for paired, and Kruskal-Wallis for ANOVA.
Here's the full cheat sheet.
Averages? One group: z or t. Two groups: two-sample or paired t. Three or more: ANOVA. Counts? Chi-square.

Quick quiz!
The same students take a test before and after coaching.
Which test checks if their scores improved?
Paired t-test!
The same students are measured twice, so each one is compared with themselves.
